subject: Copywriting
title: The First TV Commercial
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The First TV Commercial.

hook.text: On July 1, 1941, a Bulova watch ad aired before a baseball game. It lasted 10 seconds and cost $9.

buildup.text: The ad showed a clock over a map of the US with the line 'America runs on Bulova time.' Simple and direct.

discovery.text: TV changed everything. Copywriters now had to write for ears and eyes, not just the page.

twist.text: Print copywriters struggled with TV. Writing to be heard is different from writing to be read.

climax.text: A $9 ad in 1941 launched a medium that would generate $230 billion annually by 2024.

punchline.text: $9 for 10 seconds. TV ads became a $230B industry.

quiz.question: How much did the first TV commercial cost?

details.summary: The first American TV commercial aired on July 1, 1941, during a Dodgers game: a Bulova watch ad lasting 10 seconds that cost $9. details.whyItMatters: Television forced copywriters to think in pictures, sound, and motion for the first time. This multimedia shift is the direct ancestor of video advertising, social media content, and multimedia storytelling.
takeaways: The first TV ad was a 10-second Bulova watch spot in July 1941
Television required copywriters to write for sight, sound, and motion
TV advertising spending surpassed print by the late 1950s

faq.question: How did television change copywriting?
faq.answer: Print copywriters wrote for the eye alone. TV demanded scripts that combined dialogue, visual storytelling, music, and timing. The copywriter's role expanded from word-smith to storyteller. This multimedia approach now defines most digital advertising.

faq.question: Why did TV advertising grow so quickly?
faq.answer: Television offered unprecedented reach and emotional impact. Moving images combined with sound created immersive brand experiences no print ad could match. Advertisers followed audiences to the new medium, and TV ad spending exceeded print within two decades.
